narrative:
The model determined that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the first decile of your class in Year 3 is substantially lower than the average of roughly the fifth or sixth decile among students who were accepted. This single factor weighed most heavily against your application.

Your family income worked in the opposite direction. Coming from a high-income background slightly improved the model’s outlook, as this characteristic is relatively uncommon among accepted students and the model treats it as a modest positive signal.

Your LSAT score of 30 was the third most important factor. This score sits noticeably below the average of 37 among accepted applicants and therefore nudged the prediction toward a higher risk of failure, though its effect was smaller than your academic ranking.

Taken together, the model concluded your overall profile carried more risk than benefit. To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your academic performance in later years and improving your LSAT score. These two areas would have the greatest impact on moving future predictions in your favor.
